name: Mercedes-Benz eVito Panel Van
summary: A mid-size electric van with a Mercedes badge and a good cabin, but the early versions have very short range. On the used market there are two very different vans: the early 41kWh van, which has about 90 miles of official range and no rapid charging, and the later 66kWh van (60kWh usable), which has about 160 miles and CCS rapid charging. The early van only suits short, fixed urban rounds. The 66kWh van is the one most buyers should look for.

generations.label: eVito first version (41kWh)

batteries.notes: Sold as the eVito 111/112/114 e. Some ads still list 2021 vans with the 41kWh pack, so check the battery size on the V5C or spec, not just the year.

generations.dcKw: None (no rapid charging, per Driving Electric and EV database listings)
generations.notes: Motor 85kW (114hp), front-wheel drive. Not having DC charging is the big limitation.

generations.label: eVito 66kWh (later Pro/Select trims)

batteries.wltpMiles: about 159-163 (162 L2, 160 L3 per UK leasing specs)
batteries.realWorldMiles: about 120-130 (Autotrader cold test with 250kg load showed 124 miles indicated at full)
batteries.notes: Badged eVito 116 e or listed as '66kWh' in ads. Earlier trims were Progressive and Premium; later ones are Pro and Select.

generations.notes: Mercedes also made a 90kWh-usable (100kWh gross) panel van from 2025, but Auto Express reports it was not brought to the UK for lack of demand. UK ads for '100kWh' eVitos are the eVito Tourer passenger version or imports, not the panel van.

batteryWarranty: 8 years / 160,000km (about 100,000 miles), covering capacity falling below 70% (Mercedes-Benz Vans' battery certificate, as reported by UK reviews). Coverage is tied to the vehicle, so it should pass to the next owner, but check the remaining term with a Mercedes dealer using the VIN.

knownIssues.detail: The 2019-21 41kWh van has about 75-85 miles of real range and no DC charging. Reviewers list the lack of rapid charging as a main drawback.

recalls.issue: High-voltage battery housing corrosion protection may be insufficient. Fix: inspect, clean and wax the housing. Related European notices mention water getting into the battery, which can stop the van starting and raises the fire risk.
Battery management software fault that can cause loss of drive (eVito and eSprinter; reported in Germany in 2022, UK applicability not confirmed)

usedPrices: Approximate, from Autotrader UK listings and the Parkers guide (2026): 2020-21 41kWh vans cost about £9,000-£11,000. A 2021 41kWh van with 6,000 miles was listed at about £10,100 inc VAT. 66kWh vans cost about £12,000-£17,000 +VAT depending on age and mileage. Parkers values a 2020 66kWh L2 Progressive with 40k miles at about £16,700 at a dealer, and Autotrader listed a 2023 66kWh van with 17k miles at £13,499 +VAT. Prices are asking prices and approximate.
bestBuy: A 66kWh (60kWh usable) van with 80kW CCS charging, ideally 2022-on with a Mercedes dealer service history and the recall work done. The extra range and rapid charging make it far more usable than the 41kWh van for little more money.
avoid: 41kWh vans, unless your daily round is reliably under about 60 miles and you can charge at base. Also avoid a van with open battery recalls. Don't assume a '100kWh eVito' advert is a panel van: it is likely the Tourer people-carrier.
checks: Confirm battery size: 41kWh (no rapid charging) or 66kWh. The year alone does not tell you, because some 2021 vans are 41kWh.
Check the gov.uk recall checker and ask a Mercedes dealer to confirm the HV battery housing recall (2019-20 builds) and any battery software updates are done.
On a 66kWh van, test a CCS rapid charge, because DC charging is the main reason to choose it.
Ask a Mercedes dealer for the remaining battery warranty (8 years from first registration) and a battery health readout.
Check whether it is a panel van or a Tourer/crew conversion, because VAT treatment and resale differ.
confidence: medium. The battery sizes and charging figures are solid. Least certain: the exact changeover date from 41kWh to 66kWh in the UK (sources say 2021 or 2022), and whether every UK recall build range matches the European notices.

name: Mercedes-Benz eSprinter
summary: There are two completely different eSprinters. The 2020-2023 first version is a front-drive conversion with a 35kWh or 47kWh usable battery and only about 70-95 miles of range. It is cheap used, but it only suits short local work. The 2024-on version is rear-drive, with an 81kWh or 113kWh battery and up to about 270 miles WLTP. It is a genuine long-distance large van, but there are few used examples and they are expensive.

generations.label: eSprinter first generation (FWD)

batteries.notes: The common UK version, sold in L2 H2 Progressive trim, 85kW (114hp) motor.

generations.dcKw: 20 standard or 80 optional. Ads say '20kW Charger' or '80kW Charger'.
generations.notes: One body (L2 H2 high-roof panel van) was the main UK version. Payload was limited by the battery weight.

generations.label: New eSprinter (RWD, on the 'Sprinter' platform)

batteries.notes: A pre-production van covered 295 miles on one charge on a test route (Motor1). Higher-mileage summer driving gets closer to the WLTP figure.

generations.notes: A 56kWh version was announced for some markets. It is not confirmed as sold in the UK. Has a heat pump. UK prices when new were about £59k-£77k ex VAT.

batteryWarranty: 8 years / 160,000km (about 100,000 miles) to 70% capacity, per UK reviews and Mercedes vans retailers. It is attached to the vehicle, so it passes to the next owner. On early vans, check the time left, because a 2020 van's battery cover runs out in 2028.

knownIssues.issue: Very short range on first-generation vans
knownIssues.detail: With 47kWh usable and a high-roof body, the official range is only about 93-96 miles, and reviewers cite poor range as the main weakness. Don't buy one for regular motorway work.

knownIssues.issue: Slow 20kW DC charger fitted to many early vans
knownIssues.detail: Many 2020-21 vans have the 20kW DC charger, so a 'rapid' charge takes about 2 hours. Look for the '80kW Charger' in the ad title.

recalls.issue: High-voltage battery housing corrosion protection may be insufficient. Fix: inspect, clean and wax the housing. Related European notices mention water getting in, which can stop the van starting or raise the fire risk.
An HV 'battery gateway' control unit software fault can open all HV battery contactors without reason (loss of drive). Fix: software update.
Loose mounting bolts on the additional traction battery module (FWD vans). UK applicability not confirmed.

usedPrices: Approximate, from Autotrader and AutoUncle (mid/late 2026). First-generation 55kWh vans cost about £6,500-£14,000. AutoUncle's average for a Progressive is about £9,400 at about 34,500 miles. Examples: 2020 at 33k miles about £6,300-£8,500 +VAT, 2021 at 23k miles about £12,000 +VAT, and a 2022 at 17k miles about £13,500 +VAT. The 2024-on 81kWh/113kWh vans are scarce used, and asking prices are typically well above £30,000. Not enough listings to give a reliable range.
bestBuy: For short local work on a budget: a 2021-23 55kWh van with the 80kW charger, a dealer history and the battery recalls done. For real range: a 2024-on 113kWh van, if you can find one and justify the price. It is the only eSprinter that does a full day's mixed driving.
avoid: Early vans with the 20kW DC charger, if you need to top up during the day. Any first-generation van bought for long routes. Vans with outstanding HV battery recalls.
checks: Check whether it is a first-generation (FWD, 55kWh, up to 2023) or new (RWD, 81/113kWh, 2024-on) van. They are completely different vehicles.
On first-generation vans, check whether the DC charger is 20kW or 80kW. It is usually in the ad title or the spec, and it is shown on the Mercedes build data.
Run a gov.uk recall check, and ask a Mercedes dealer to confirm the HV battery housing and battery gateway software recalls are done.
Work out the years left on the 8-year battery warranty from the first registration date. 2020 vans run out in 2028.
Check the payload on the plate. The first-generation van's battery weight cuts the payload, especially on converted bodies.
confidence: medium. The first-generation specs, the 20/80kW charger split and the recalls are solid. Least certain: real-world range for the 81kWh van, whether a 56kWh version is sold in the UK, and used prices for the 2024-on van.

name: Iveco eDaily
summary: An electric version of the body-on-frame Daily, sold as a van or chassis cab from 3.5t up to 7.2t. It has modular 37kWh battery packs, so range depends entirely on how many packs a van has. It suits heavy-payload, conversion and tipper/Luton work better than most electric vans. Used examples are fairly rare, so specs vary widely.

generations.label: eDaily (MY22, with a MY24 update adding a fourth pack)

batteries.notes: 100kW motor version (35S10). No DC charging, per Parkers.

batteries.realWorldMiles: about 120-145 (twin-battery test drive about 146 miles claimed)

batteries.wltpMiles: up to about 186 (4.25t+, twin rear wheel)

batteries.notes: Added with the 2024 update, heavy chassis versions.

generations.dcKw: 80 (2-3 pack versions). None on the 37kWh single pack.
generations.notes: 3.5t vans take one or two packs only. Iveco quotes the WLTP figures at a full payload, so they are lower than most rivals' figures.

batteryWarranty: 8 years / 155,000 miles for two- or three-pack vans, and 8 years / 100,000 miles for single-pack vans, to 80% of original capacity, per UK reviews and leasing specs. The base vehicle warranty is 3 years / 100,000 miles. Check with an Iveco dealer whether the battery cover transfers and how much is left.

knownIssues.detail: The 37kWh version has no DC charging and a low real range, so it suits depot-based vans only. Check the pack count before buying.

usedPrices: Not enough electric-specific UK listings to give a reliable range (late 2026). Most used 'Daily' listings are diesel. Expect very wide variation by body (van, tipper, Luton), battery count and GVW. Check Autotrader with the fuel type filtered to electric.
bestBuy: A 3.5t 74kWh (twin-pack) van with 80kW DC charging. It is the best balance of range and payload for licence-B drivers. For heavier bodies, a 4.25t+ 111kWh chassis.
avoid: Single-pack 37kWh vans, unless the work is very short-range with depot charging. Vans above 3.5t, unless drivers have the right licence (C1) or meet the rules for electric vans up to 4.25t on a car licence.
checks: Count the battery packs (37/74/111/148kWh). Range, DC charging and battery warranty mileage all depend on it.
Check the GVW plate. Vans over 3.5t need a C1 licence unless they meet the alternative-fuel rules for up to 4.25t.
On converted bodies (tipper, Luton, refrigerated), get the converter's paperwork and check whether the body is powered from the HV system.
Check the gov.uk recall service and ask an Iveco dealer for the software update history.
Confirm the remaining battery warranty and the 80% capacity threshold with Iveco.
confidence: low-medium. The battery modules and warranty are fairly solid. Least certain: real-world range, UK used prices (almost no data) and DVSA recalls (none found).

name: Maxus eDeliver 9
summary: A Transit-sized electric large van that was much cheaper than the European brands when new. That makes it one of the cheapest ways into a big used electric van. Range varies a lot by battery size, from about 112 to 219 miles WLTP. The front-wheel-drive layout and lots of standard equipment are pluses. The dealer network and resale values are the weak points.

generations.label: eDeliver 9

batteries.notes: Later UK price lists and ads show 65kWh (chassis cab/Luton) and 77kWh versions. Exact specs not confirmed.

generations.dcKw: about 80 (0-80% in about 40-45 minutes, per Maxus)
generations.notes: 150kW motor, front-wheel drive. Sold as a panel van (MWB/LWB, various roofs), chassis cab and Luton.

batteryWarranty: 8 years / 100,000 miles is the most consistently reported figure (one leasing source says 150,000). The vehicle warranty is 5 years, with reports of 60,000 miles or 125,000 miles. Check the terms and transfer with a Maxus dealer (Harris Maxus is the UK distributor).

knownIssues.detail: WLTP range runs from 112 miles (51.5kWh) to 219 miles (88.5kWh). The ad title doesn't always state the battery, so check the V5C or spec.

recalls.issue: The handbrake cable's yellow plastic ferrule can fail, giving excess handbrake travel and letting the van move unexpectedly

usedPrices: Approximate, from Autotrader and AutoUncle (2026). 2022 72kWh vans with about 28k miles cost about £11,000 +VAT. A 2023 88.5kWh van with about 32k miles was listed at about £13,500 +VAT. 2024 72kWh vans with low miles cost about £17,750 +VAT. Nearly new 2025 Lutons cost up to about £36,500. Prices fell steeply from new, which makes these vans good value but means resale will be weak too.
bestBuy: An 88.5kWh panel van from 2022-on, with the handbrake recall done and a Maxus dealer history. It has more than 50% more range than the 72kWh van for a small price difference used.
avoid: 51.5kWh vans, unless the work is short-range. Any 2019-22 build without proof the handbrake recall was done.
checks: Confirm the battery size (51.5/72/88.5kWh, or the later 65/77kWh) from the V5C or Maxus build data.
Check the handbrake recall (2019-22 builds) on the gov.uk service. Test the handbrake on a slope: excess lever travel is the warning sign.
Find your nearest Maxus service dealer before buying, because the network is thinner than Ford's or Mercedes'.
Test a CCS rapid charge, and check that the infotainment and charging-schedule software has been updated by a dealer.
Check the remaining battery warranty (8 years from first registration) with a Maxus dealer.
confidence: medium. The original three batteries, WLTP figures and the handbrake recall are solid. Least certain: the later 65/77kWh versions, the exact DC peak rate, the vehicle warranty mileage and real-world range (no UK test found).

name: Maxus eDeliver 7
summary: A medium van (Transit Custom size) launched in 2023/24. It has big batteries and up to about 220-230 miles WLTP, for a lower price than mainstream rivals. Used supply is thin and mostly low-mileage ex-demonstrator or pre-registered stock. It is an interesting value buy if there is a Maxus dealer nearby.

generations.label: eDeliver 7
generations.notes: 150kW motor, one well-equipped trim. Launch price from about £45,000 ex VAT.

batteryWarranty: Not confirmed specifically for this model. Maxus normally quotes 8 years / 100,000 miles on the battery for its electric vans. Check with a Maxus dealer.
usedPrices: Approximate, from Autotrader and dealer listings (2026), and only a few examples. Low-mileage 2024-25 77kWh vans are listed at about £21,000-£29,000 +VAT, and a 2025 88.5kWh van at about £24,000 +VAT. Pricing is inconsistent between trade and retail sites.
bestBuy: An 88kWh version, nearly new, from a Maxus dealer with the remaining warranty. Used prices are close to the 77kWh van's.
checks: Confirm the battery size (77 or 88kWh) and the body length (L1/L2).
Find your nearest Maxus service dealer before buying.
Check whether it was a pre-registered or ex-demo van, and get the warranty start date.
Test a rapid charge and the dealer software status.
confidence: low-medium. The battery sizes and DC rate are solid. Least certain: the exact WLTP figures (sources say 224-230 miles), battery warranty terms, and used prices from a tiny sample.

name: Maxus eDeliver 3
summary: A small, cheap electric van. It has decent payload (about 865-905kg) and modest range. As a used buy it is one of the cheapest electric vans around, and it suits local trades and urban delivery. The cabin and refinement are basic, and dealer support is thinner than for the big brands. Used vans are listed regularly, but it is unclear whether it is still sold new in the UK (the eDeliver 5 has joined the range).

generations.label: eDeliver 3 (SWB L1 panel van in the UK; LWB and chassis versions in some markets)
generations.dcKw: Not confirmed. 0-80% in about 45 minutes on a DC charger for either battery, per Maxus. Peak DC rate not confirmed (reports range from about 28kW to 50kW+).

batteryWarranty: 8 years / 100,000 miles reported by UK dealers (some other markets differ). Check transfer and remaining term with a Maxus dealer.
usedPrices: Approximate. Parkers' guide shows about £7,500-£19,000. Autotrader stock is thin (under 50 vans at a time). Older 35kWh vans sit at the bottom of that range.
bestBuy: The 52.5kWh version. Its range is about 50% better for little extra cost used, and the payload is slightly higher.
avoid: 35kWh vans, if you regularly do more than about 70 miles a day.
checks: Confirm the battery size (35 or 52.5kWh). They look identical.
Find your nearest Maxus service dealer before buying.
Test a DC rapid charge and note the charge rate, because the peak DC rate is modest.
Check the gov.uk recall service and the dealer service history.
Check body panels and the load area for damage, and ask a Maxus dealer about parts lead times before buying a damaged van.
confidence: low-medium. Battery options and payload are solid. Least certain: the DC peak rate, the WLTP figures (sources differ), whether it is still on sale new.

name: LEVC VN5
summary: A van version of the London black cab. It is a plug-in electric van with a small 1.5-litre petrol engine that only acts as a generator and never drives the wheels. It does about 60 miles WLTP on battery alone and about 300 miles in total, so there is no range anxiety. It is cheap used, but the load floor is high and load space is smaller than rivals'. It suits mixed urban and longer work where charging is unreliable.

generations.label: VN5 (range-extended electric)

batteries.wltpMiles: 61 electric-only; about 300+ total with the range extender
batteries.notes: Petrol 1.5 turbo three-cylinder generator. Fuel use about 6.9 l/100km once the battery is depleted (German test).

generations.acKw: Not confirmed (11kW and 22kW AC versions are listed in Parkers' trims)
generations.dcKw: Not confirmed (believed to be about 50kW CCS)
generations.notes: How it differs: it needs petrol and oil servicing as well as EV checks. Check clean-air zone and congestion charge status for your area, because it has a petrol engine. It has a high load floor and a payload of about 830kg. Drive modes (Pure EV / Save / Smart) control when the generator runs.

batteryWarranty: 8 years / 150,000 miles drive-battery warranty as standard (extended option 8 years / 200,000 miles), per LEVC's warranty page. Check the transfer and remaining term with LEVC.

knownIssues.issue: High load floor and compromised load space
knownIssues.detail: The range-extender layout raises the floor. Reviewers rate practicality poorly.

recalls.issue: One UK recall is recorded for the VN5 on a third-party aggregator. Details not confirmed, so check by VIN on gov.uk.

usedPrices: Approximate, from Autotrader, AutoUncle and the AA (2026). 2021 vans cost about £10,000 +VAT (38k miles). 2022 vans cost about £11,000-£14,000 and 2023 vans about £12,000-£14,700. The Parkers guide covers about £5,400-£21,500 across all.
bestBuy: A 2022-23 VN5 with a full LEVC service history (including the petrol generator) and plenty of battery warranty left. Ideal if you can't rely on charging every day.
avoid: Vans driven mostly on petrol (high miles, little charging), because they lose the cost advantage. Any van with a patchy generator service history.
checks: Check the service history for both the EV system and the petrol generator (oil changes, etc.).
Ask how it was used: mostly electric or mostly generator. Trip data or fuel receipts help.
Check the load floor height and load length suit your work, because it is smaller inside than a Vivaro-sized van.
Check the electric-only range on a full charge on your test drive (expect about 50-60 miles).
Check eligibility for any clean-air zone, congestion charge or grant scheme you rely on, because it has a petrol engine.
confidence: medium. The battery, range and warranty are solid. Least certain: the AC/DC charge rates, recall details, whether it is still sold new, and the clean-air zone/grant status.

name: Kia PV5 Cargo
summary: A new compact-to-medium electric van built from the ground up on Kia's dedicated van platform. It went on sale in the UK in 2025. Reviewers praise its efficiency and value. There is very little used supply so far, mainly nearly-new stock, so used pricing is not yet established.

generations.label: PV5 Cargo
generations.notes: Launch prices from about £27,645 ex VAT before the grant.

batteryWarranty: 7 years / 100,000 miles vehicle warranty. The battery has its own 8-year cover (mileage limit not confirmed). The warranty transfers to the next owner.

recalls.issue: Possible faulty weld on the front-right suspension strut bracket (KBA, Germany). UK applicability not confirmed.
Bonnet material structure may raise pedestrian injury risk (KBA). UK applicability not confirmed.
Seatbelt fastening bolts (small campaign). UK applicability not confirmed.

usedPrices: Used examples are rare. Not enough listings to give a reliable range (late 2026).
bestBuy: A nearly-new Long Range (71.2kWh) van with most of the 7-year warranty left.
checks: Check the gov.uk recall service and a Kia dealer for the 2025-26 recalls (suspension strut weld, bonnet, seatbelt bolts).
Confirm Standard (51.5kWh) or Long Range (71.2kWh). The payload differs by about 100kg.
Confirm the warranty start date.
confidence: medium on specs, low on used market. Least certain: whether the European recalls apply to UK vans, and the battery warranty mileage.

name: Farizon SV
summary: A large electric van from Geely's commercial brand, on sale in the UK since 2025 through Jameel Motors. It has big batteries and decent rapid charging, and was cheap when new. Used supply is minimal, and the dealer network is still young.

generations.label: SV
generations.notes: 20-80% in about 36 minutes on the 83kWh, per Farizon. New price about £44,000-£55,000 ex VAT.

batteryWarranty: 8 years / 120,000 miles battery warranty. The vehicle warranty is 4 years / 120,000 miles (one source says 125,000).
usedPrices: Used examples are rare. Not enough listings to give a reliable price range (late 2026).
checks: Check where your nearest Farizon service dealer is, because the network is still small.
Confirm the battery (67/83/106kWh) and the body size.
Confirm the warranty start date and the dealer servicing record.
confidence: medium on specs, low on used market. Least certain: the exact WLTP figures per body, and the warranty mileage.

name: Citroën ë-C3 Van
summary: A small car-derived van based on the ë-C3 hatchback, on sale in the UK from mid-2025. It has a 44kWh battery and about 200 miles WLTP, but only a car-sized load area (about 1.2 cubic metres) and about 300kg payload. It suits light-parcel or mobile service work. Used examples are rare.

generations.label: ë-C3 Van

batteries.notes: Battery chemistry not confirmed for the van.

generations.acKw: 7.4 (as listed in the e-C3 car spec)
generations.notes: Payload about 300kg, load volume about 1,220 litres. Launch price about £22,400 ex VAT before the grant.

knownIssues.detail: About 300kg payload. Reviewers say the conversion looks a little amateur in places.

usedPrices: Used examples are rare. Not enough listings to give a reliable range (late 2026).
avoid: Don't buy it if you need more than about 300kg payload or a full-size load bay.
checks: Check the payload against your typical load: about 300kg including any racking.
Check the gov.uk recall service.
Confirm the warranty start date.
confidence: medium on specs, low on used market. Least certain: the battery warranty, the AC charge rate on the van, and the battery chemistry.
